job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

passage: Teacher: Today we are discussing how globalisation shapes our economy. Rahul, do you think MNCs only operate from their home countries? Rahul: I thought they only produced goods in their home country, like the USA. Teacher: Actually, MNCs set up production units globally to reduce costs. Priya, what about trade barriers? Priya: I believe removing trade barriers always helps every local producer by increasing their sales. Teacher: Not necessarily. While it opens markets, small producers often struggle to compete with cheaper imports. Rahul: Is globalisation just a natural, unstoppable force? Teacher: No, it is shaped by government policy. Through liberalisation, governments decide how much to open their markets. Priya: And the WTO ensures fairness, right? Teacher: The WTO aims to liberalise trade, but it is not a perfectly democratic body where all countries have equal power. Developed nations often exert more influence over its rules. Globalisation is a complex process influenced by both private corporations and state decisions, rather than being an automatic phenomenon beyond human control. By understanding these policies, we can see how trade integration impacts different sectors of the Indian economy differently. It is not a simple win for everyone, nor is it an uncontrollable wave.

items.evidence: Teacher: Actually, MNCs set up production units globally to reduce costs.
items.q: An American company wants to cut its production costs. What is it most likely to do?
options: Open factories in several other countries
Keep all of its production inside the USA
Make everything at home, then ship it abroad
Close its units abroad to save on costs
items.explain: MNCs set up production units around the world to reduce costs, not only at home.

wrong.why: thinks MNCs only produce in their home country
thinks goods are made in one place and shipped
reverses the cause: thinks going global raises costs

items.evidence: While it opens markets, small producers often struggle to compete with cheaper imports.
items.q: India removes import taxes on toys. What will happen to small Indian toy makers?
options: They will find it hard to beat cheap imports
They will sell many more toys than before
They alone will gain, not the toy buyers
They will be kept safe by fair WTO rules
items.explain: Open markets bring cheaper imports, and small producers often struggle to compete with them.

wrong.why: thinks removing barriers always helps local producers
thinks the WTO is fair to everyone

items.evidence: Through liberalisation, governments decide how much to open their markets.
items.q: Two countries allow very different amounts of foreign trade. Which explains this difference?
options: Each government chooses its own trade policy
Globalisation is a natural force nobody controls
The WTO forced each one to open in 1947
Big companies alone set every country's trade rules
items.explain: Through liberalisation, each government decides how far to open its markets, so countries differ.

wrong.why: thinks globalisation cannot be shaped by policy
thinks the WTO forced India to open in 1947
ignores the role of state decisions

items.evidence: Developed nations often exert more influence over its rules.
items.q: A poor and a rich country disagree over a WTO rule. Whose view usually wins?
options: The developed country, as it has more influence
Neither country, as all have equal power
The poorer country, as the WTO protects it
The country that opens its markets the most
items.explain: The WTO is not perfectly democratic; developed nations often have more influence over its rules.

wrong.why: thinks all WTO members have equal power
reverses who holds influence in the WTO
thinks fairness is about opening markets equally
